key_bets: Electron co-confinement in the crossed-field Orbitron geometry enables ion densities ~50× above the space-charge limit (currently supported by PIC simulations only)
Coulomb collision thermalization can be suppressed sufficiently to allow Q>1 operation, despite the 1998 Lampe-Mannheimer analysis claiming collision rates 25–37× faster than fusion
Sustained 300 kV operation with 4.7 MV/m field gradient can be maintained reliably under D-T plasma load and neutron bombardment over commercial timescales
Mass-manufactured small modules (1–100 kWe each) can be stacked into a commercial plant architecture at low per-kWe capital cost
A practical energy conversion pathway exists for kWe-scale modules, despite conventional thermal turbines being impractical below ~1 MWe
HTS superconducting magnet upgrade to 0.5 T can be achieved in compact geometry adjacent to a neutron-producing device
Ion orbit stability at 300 kV is achievable without ion-cathode impact at fusion-relevant kinetic energies
eliminated_costs: Large superconducting magnet systems — only a small 0.5 T HTS coil pair required vs. 5–20 T fields in MFE tokamaks, avoiding the REBCO tape supply bottleneck
Breeding blanket capital cost — no FLiBe or LiPb blanket required at current design maturity (replaced by purchased tritium OPEX)
Conventional plasma heating systems — no RF, NBI, or gyrotron systems; replaced by HV power supply plus ion gun array
Large beryllium inventories and FLiBe production requirements are avoided entirely
Large-volume first wall and divertor systems sized for a single large plasma are replaced by per-module chamber components
novel_costs: Sustained 300 kV HV power supply and proprietary HV feedthrough at per-module scale, scaling with module count across the plant
Purchased tritium as a permanent OPEX driver at >$35,000/g (no breeding blanket design exists; MoU with Fusion Fuel Cycles covers this only as a collaboration direction)
Per-module neutron shielding (the 'concrete castle' approach) for stacked multi-module arrays — economically unfavorable at small module scale
Cathode replacement cost under combined neutron and ion bombardment, with unknown lifetime driving variable O&M
Energy conversion at 1–100 kWe module scale where conventional turbines are impractical and thermoelectric efficiency is only ~5–15%

risks.description: Q>1 has not been demonstrated in any electrostatic confinement device; the entire economic case is conditional on an unproven physics result
Coulomb collision loss rate is unmeasured at fusion-relevant parameters; the 1998 Lampe-Mannheimer analysis claims rates 25–37× faster than fusion — an unresolved fundamental barrier
The central 50× density-enhancement claim is supported only by PIC simulations; space-charge mitigation is explicitly stated as 'the focus of initial experiments' and not yet achieved
No commercial plant architecture exists — module count, BOP layout, shielding integration, and tritium handling across hundreds of modules are entirely undefined
Energy conversion pathway at 1–100 kWe module scale is undefined; stated turbines are impractical below ~1 MWe and no alternative is specified
No breeding blanket design exists; tritium must be purchased indefinitely at >$35,000/g, potentially adding $0.01–0.10/kWh and dominating OPEX at near-breakeven Q
Diocotron and electron cyclotron drift instabilities are identified in simulations but uncharacterized experimentally, creating risk at higher density operation
Cathode and HV feedthrough lifetime under sustained 14 MeV neutron bombardment is uncharacterized, driving unknown maintenance cycles and replacement costs
Overnight capital cost per kWe is entirely unbounded — the aspirational <$1B figure has no cost basis and no plant study exists
Ion orbit stability at 300 kV under D-T plasma conditions has not been demonstrated; ion-cathode impact at fusion-relevant energies is a structural concern raised in external critique
Per-kWe labor and O&M costs are highly unfavorable at 1–100 kWe module scale — a technician visit costs the same regardless of module output
Scaling law from demonstrated 100 kV operation to the 300 kV target operating point is not publicly validated (accessible only as abstract)
Avalanche Energy is a small early-stage company with modest funding ($29M Series A + $10M state grant) relative to the scale of physics and engineering challenges
Regulatory cost exposure under a fission-style regime (Stewart & Shirvan 2.2× building cost factor) would apply if scaled to commercial power plant operation
